title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Use the language of criticality, choosing words that show how your ideas relate rather than just listing them.

title: Words that do more than connect
body: Some words in academic writing only join sentences together. Others show the reader exactly how two ideas relate, contrast, build, or follow from each other. That second group is the language of criticality.

title: The book's own examples
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.129-131) point to words such as 'although', 'in addition', and 'therefore' as signals of this kind, noting that further examples are set out in the book's own Table 8.2. Each of these words commits you to a specific relationship between two ideas, not just their presence together.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two sentences reporting the same two findings.

{{learner-a}} strings two findings together with 'and': 'Smith found X, and Jones found Y.'

{{learner-b}} writes the same two findings with 'although': 'Although Smith found X, Jones found Y', signalling a contrast the reader is meant to notice.

Both sentences were accurate. Only {{learner-b}}'s sentence told the reader how the findings related.

title: Why the choice of word is a critical choice
body: Choosing 'although' over 'and' is not a style preference. It is a claim about how two ideas relate, and getting it wrong misrepresents the relationship between your sources just as much as getting a fact wrong would.

title: Three connecting words, defined
instruction: Select each highlighted word to see the relationship it signals.

_passage.text: Three words carry particular weight in critical writing:

_term.definition: Signals a contrast: the idea that follows runs against what the reader might expect from the idea before it.
Signals that a further, separate point is being added, not a conclusion drawn from what came before.
Signals a conclusion: the idea that follows is being drawn as a consequence of what came before, not simply added to it.

_passage.text: . Choosing between them is choosing what relationship you are claiming between two ideas.

title: Match the word to the relationship
displayTitle: What relationship does each word signal?
body: Each connecting word commits you to a specific relationship between two ideas. Match each word to what it signals.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Match each connecting word to the relationship it signals.

title: Choosing deliberately
body: Before you join two sentences with 'and', ask what relationship actually holds between them. If it is a contrast, a consequence, or an addition, say so. The book's Table 8.2 is worth keeping open while you redraft a section this way.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Find a sentence in your own writing joined with 'and'. What relationship was actually there: contrast, addition, or consequence?
Which connecting word would make that relationship explicit?
